
# Language

## What is language

Finite system of symbols (words) that can be combined using rules to make a virtually infinite number of distinct sentences.

* Unique to humans, who are predisposed to acquire it
* Basic function underlying language are largely shared with non-human animals

## What is language

Finite system of [symbols]{style="background: black; color: white"} (words) that can be combined using rules to make a virtually infinite number of distinct sentences.

# Language in the brain

## Basic brain anatomy

<https://atlases.ebrains.eu/viewer/>

<https://www.brainfacts.org/3d-brain>

![Brain macro-anatomy](/img/brain-macro.png){ #fig-brain-macro }

## Language impairments (aphasia)


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

The first **neuroanatomical mapping** of language functions (*speaking*, *understanding*, *reading*, *writing*) came from clinical studies on patients with **brain lesions** and language impairments.

:::

::: {.column}

Aphasia
: Aphasia is a disorder that results from damage (usually from a stroke or traumatic brain injury) to areas of the brain that are responsible for language.^[NIH, <https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/aphasia>]

:::

:::

## Language impairments (aphasia)

 
::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

**Acquired brain damage** after stroke damage (most common), head injury, progressive neurological disorders (e.g., Alzheimer), brain tumor, encephalitis.

Damage is more frequently located on **left side of the brain**.

Can affect one or more communication modalities:

|          | *Comprehension*      | *Production*      |
|----------|----------------------|-------------------|
|*Spoken*  | Speech comprehension | Speech production |
|*Written* | Reading              | Writing           |
:::

::: {.column}

![Lesion overlap map for 69 patients with left hemisphere post stroke aphasia<br>[@halai2020investigating]](/img/halai2021.jpeg)

:::

:::


## Language impairments (aphasia)

Localization of the damage is associated with different resulting patterns of language impairment.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A[Is fluent] --> B[Can comprehend]
  A --> C[Cannot comprehend]
  B --> E[Can repeat]
  B --> F[Cannot repeat]
  C --> G[Can repeat]
  C --> H[Cannot repeat]
  I[Is not fluent] --> J[Can comprehend]
  I --> K[Cannot comprehend]
  J --> L[Can repeat]
  J --> M[Cannot repeat]
  K --> N[Can repeat]
  K --> O[Cannot repeat]
  
  E --> P(Anomic aphasia)
  F --> Q(Conduction aphasia)
  G --> R(Transcortical<br>sensory aphasia)
  H --> S(Wernicke's aphasia)
  L --> T(Transcortical<br>motor aphasia)
  M --> U(Broca's aphasia)
  N --> V(Mixed transcortical<br>aphasia)
  O --> W(Global aphasia)


```

## Broca's aphasia

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

Paul Broca (1861)

* Inability to properly **produce** any words other than "tan".
* Speech comprehension intact
* Post-mortem examination of the patient's brain: damage to the 3rd convolution of the left frontal lobe

This area is now known as Broca's Area, and corresponds to Broadmann's area BA 44/45
:::

::: {.column}

![Copyright © Society for Neuroscience (2017).](/img/broca.jpg)

:::

:::

## Broca's aphasia

* Difficulties in **speech production**
* **Speech comprehension** intact

What can we learn from the function of Broca's area? Broca's area involved in:

* **Motor programing** of **articulatory movements** (together with supplementary motor area, basal ganglia and cerebellum)
* **Grammatical processing** (activates when judging the grammaticality of a sentence)

## Broca's aphasia


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

>Yes... ah... Monday... er... Dad and Peter H... (his own name), and Dad.... er... hospital... and ah... Wednesday... Wednesday, nine o'clock... and oh... Thursday... ten o'clock, ah doctors... two... an' doctors... and er... teeth...yah.

:::

::: {.column}

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JWC-cVQmEmY width="500" height="500" >}}

:::

:::


## Wernicke's aphasia
 
::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

Carl Wenicke (1874):

* Difficulties in understanding language
* Fluent speech, typical speech rate, intact grammatical abilities
* Produced speech does not have meaning (*word salad*)
* Post-mortem examination of the patient's brain: left temporal lobe

This area is now known as Wernickes's area, and corresponds to Broadmann's area BA 22/24.
:::

::: {.column}

![Copyright © Society for Neuroscience (2017).](/img/wernicke.jpg)

:::

:::


## Wernicke's aphasia
 
::: {.columns}

::: {.column}


Wernickes's area involved in:

* Speech comprehension
* Close to auditory cortex
* Involved in access to word meaning

:::

::: {.column}

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3oef68YabD0 width="500" height="500" >}}
:::

:::

## Conduction aphasia

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

@brookshire2014introduction:

* **Deficit in spoken word repetition**: patients fail to encode phonological information (inverted positions of syllables)
* Speech comprehension relatively preseved
* Patients are aware of the errors (unlike other forms of aphasia) but still have difficulty in correcting their speech
* Lesion in the arcuate fasciculus, often after stroke

This area is now known as Wernickes's area, and corresponds to Broadmann's area BA 22/24.
:::

::: {.column}

![Wikimedia Commons](/img/arcuate.jpg)

:::

:::

## Conduction aphasia

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}


> *Clinician*: Now, I want you to say some words after me. Say 'boy'.

> *Patient*: Boy.

> *Clinician*: Let's try another one. Say 'refrigerator'.

> *Patient*: Frigilator … no? how about … frerigilator … no frigaliterlater… aahh! It's all mixed up!" 

:::

::: {.column}

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1yC-uX5VOiE width="600" height="400" >}}

:::

:::


## Anomic aphasia and primary progressive aphasia (PPA)

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

@brookshire2014introduction:

* **Difficulty in word selection** of (nouns and verbs): failed word retrieval
* Fluent speech
* Comprehension preserved
* Can be very specific: color anomia (deficit in retrieving words for color)
* Neuroanatomical correlates unclear: **Peri-sylvian area**, generally result of progressive diseases

:::

::: {.column}

![Magnetic resonance imaging 10-year clinical course of PPA patient with pure anomic aphasia showing progressive atrophy of the left temporal lobe, eventually spread bilaterally.](/img/ota2024.jpg)

:::

:::


## Global aphasia

* Serious **deficit of speech production and comprehension**
* Patients are almost mute or produced stereotyped sentences (formed by very few disconnected words)
* Repetitions, reading, writing all compromised patients are able to express themselves using intonation, facial expression, gestures

* Lesion at left inferior frontal areas, superior temporal areas, most of the parietal lobe
* Typically caused by occlusion (thrombotic stroke) at the left middle cerebral artery [@alexander1992lesion]

## Brain localization of language functions

### Lateralization

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}


* Many human cognitive functions are *lateralized*: brain shows functional asymmetries (one hemisphere is specialized in processing a given type of information)
* Cerebral hemispheres are interconnected by the corpus callosum: largest fiber system in the brain!

:::

::: {.column}

![](/img/lateralization.png)

:::

:::

## Brain localization of language functions

### Lateralization: Corpus callosum

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

* These fibers connect correspondent brain areas in the two hemispheres (homotopic connection), but also non-correspondent areas (heterotopic connections)
* Main function: inhibitory role; it prevents competition between brain hemispheres in information processing

:::

::: {.column}

![](/img/lateralization.png)

:::

:::

## Lateralization of language functions

### Lateralization: Corpus callosum

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

* Corpus callosum matures slowly over the first 5 to 10 years of human life 
* Resection of corpus callosum or hemispherectomy in case of severe epilepsy in children under this age does not compromise the brain 
* Brain rewires itself! 

:::

::: {.column}

![](/img/half.png)

:::

:::

## Brain localization of language functions

### Lateralization: Wada's test

Wada test or Wada-Milner test (1930)

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

* Injection of anesthetic agent into the internal carotid artery to **anesthetize one hemisphere at a time**
* Used to **determine cerebral dominance** for language functions invasive and risky

:::

::: {.column}

![](/img/wada.png)

:::

:::

## Brain localization of language functions

### Lateralization: Wada's test

Wada test or Wada-Milner test (1930)

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

Injection in the dominant hemisphere for language causes speech arrest or language impairments but not when injections was performed in the non-dominant hemisphere.

* Use for research now replaced with safer techniques
* Still used with some patients in need of brain surgery
:::

::: {.column}

![](/img/wada.png)

:::

:::

## Brain localization of language functions

### Lateralization: Neuroimaging

For many years the preferred hand was believed to be contralateral to the cerebral hemisphere dominant for language:

* Right-handers → left-hemisphere dominance
* Left-handers → right-hemisphere dominance

**Now**: brain lateralization is ***partially*** associated with handedness

* Right-handers → 95% have left-hemisphere dominance for language
* Left-handers → 50-70% also show left-hemisphere dominance

Hand preference is relevant but not totally reliable as predicting measure of language dominance in the brain.

# Spoken speech perception

From sound to meaning.

## Structure of the speech signal

![Oscillogram of a spoken sentence in Spanish.](/img/signal.png)

## Structure of the speech signal

![Oscillogram of a spoken sentence in Spanish (segmented).](/img/signal-segmented.png)

## Structure of the speech signal

**Continuous signal** with no silent pauses between words

Boundaries between individual spoken words are not easy to detect:

> "ice cream" vs. "I scream"

<br>
Speech segmentation
: Identifying word boundaries in continuous speech, when a word begins and ends

## Structure of the speech signal

### Speech segmentation


Through **exposure to language**, learners detect the likelihood (probabilities) with which sounds go together 

Sounds that often appear together are more likely to form a word (*ho-la* → *hola*) 

Human infants learning native language(s) use the same mechanism in order to predict what sound comes next.

## Structure of the speech signal

### Speech segmentation

{{< video https://vimeo.com/21454995 width="900" height="500" >}}

## Structure of the speech signal

### Variability in speech

Inter-speaker differences: the same speech sound, syllable or word sounds different depending on many factors.

* **Age**: kids' voice is different than adults' voice in many dimensions (e.g., pitch, intonation)
* **Sex**: female voice has higher pitch than male voice
* **Accent**: variations in pronunciation e.g., American vs. British English
* **Dialect**: variations in grammar and vocabulary; e.g., different words to express the same content

## Structure of the speech signal

### Variability in speech

Inter-speaker differences: the same speech sound, syllable or word sounds different depending on many factors.

This does not stop us from identifying the same words and activating the same meanings!

## Structure of the speech signal

### Variability in speech

**Development**: 9-month-old infants fail to recognize the same word when pronounced by speakers using different dialects

**Experience**: Similar effects in adults learning new languages

How do language learners deal with variability in the input?

Through increased exposure to language, we learn that some sets of properties are more constant than others (e.g., sounds of the same word go together no matter who is talking)

We consider such regular properties a more reliable source of information, and ignore (although not completely) other sources

Netflix documentary Babies, Episode 'First Words'

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BFtbXwnBRg8>

## Brain correlates of spoken speech perception

### 1) Auditory nerve (cochlear nerve)

Carries out sensory info from the ear to the brain, through the auditory pathway, reaching out  the primary auditory cortex (A1), located in temporal lobes.

Contralateral projections of the two ears to project to the opposite hemisphere (left ear's nerve projects to the right temporal lobe and viceversa).

## Brain underpinnings

### 2) Auditory cortex

Primary auditory cortex responds equally to speech and other sounds in both left and right hemisphere.

However, anterior regions of left auditory cortex responds more to speech than non-speech sounds with same acoustic complexity (Scott et al., 2000)

Right hemisphere does not show this preference, suggesting specialization of left hemisphere for speech processing.

Left hemisphere damages can result in a type of auditory agnosia = environmental sounds and music are identified, but not speech (which appears "distorted and too fast"

## Brain underpinnings

### 2) Auditory cortex

advantage of right auditory pathway, that projects contralaterally to the left hemisphere in processing spoken language

Dichotic listening: when two different linguistic sounds (e.g., syllables or words) are presented simultaneously to both ears, the sound coming from the right ear arrives faster at Wernicke's area

when there is acoustic competition, participants repeat the syllables presented to the right ear more accurately  

# Visual speech perception (reading)

From text to meaning

## Literacy

the ability to read and write is essentially a cultural invention albeit of great significance;   

ability to use printed and written materials (language, numbers, computer scripts) to gain knowledge 

pre-historic literacy = earliest form of written communication dates back to 3500 BCE, in Sumer (southern Mesopotamia)  

literacy became universal in Western cultures 100 years ago; for 95% of our history the Homo Sapiens was pre-literate

## Literacy

![](/img/literacy.png)

## Literacy

reading and writing are astonishing complex skills

learning to read and write requires a dedicated neuro-cognitive system which comprises other perceptual and cognitive functions: 

* basic visual skills (visual recognition)
* phonological processing (knowledge of the sounds of language)
* oculomotor control (ability to control eye movements)
* attention
* memory
* learning
* high-level language capacities to detect meanings 
* human brain has not evolved specifically for literacy, we have to learn it!

## READING AS LEARNED EXPERT SYSTEM

visual word recognition = how we recognize individual printed words
cognitive mechanism that allows reader to map orthography (printed words) into phonology (sounds) 
computational models provide useful info to understand how reading works 
artificial neural networks – the most used models that simulate how brain neurons respond during reading 

## READING AS LEARNED EXPERT SYSTEM

word superiority effect = detection of a single letter (R) is faster in the context of a word (CARPET) or plausible non-word (HARPOT) than a random string of letter (CTRPAE)
visual word recognition does not work letter-by-letter 
our brain is likely to process clusters of letters (the word as a whole) rather than individual letters

## READING AS LEARNED EXPERT SYSTEM

![](/img/read.png)

## Characteristics of VWFA

## Reading impairments

### Pure alexia

severe reading problems, patients read letter-by-letter 
impairment of the parallel processing of letters
reading difficulty increases with word length
other language skills are intact but naming is also impaired, especially for colors

## Reading impairments

### Pure alexia

principally caused by infarct to the left posterior cerebral artery, that perfuses corpus callosum and left visual cortex 

damage at inferior longitudinal fasciculus that connects VWFA to occipital lobe, impairing transmission of visual info to VWFA

## Reading impairments

### Pure alexia

patients can still write because pathways connecting left-sided language areas to motor areas are intact
rehabilitation may work (e.g., reading out loud to stimulate the damaged system in the brain)
other associated signs: short-term memory loss, hemianopia (blindess over half vision field)
controversy about whether the deficit impairs general visual processing or reading-specific mechanisms or both (problems at one level would affect the other, and vice versa)

## Reading impairments

### Acquired surface dislexia

mispronunciation of irregular words = patients read all words following standard pronunciation rules
regularization errors: patients cannot recognize a word as a whole, and retrieve pronunciation from memory, e.g., shoe = /sho/ as in show
principal damage in left occipito-temporal area (VWFA)

## Reading impairments

### Acquired phonological dislexia

inability to read non-words ---> opposite of Surface Dyslexia
ability to read words is not impaired
sometimes the distinction is more accurate and points to the familiarity of the word = phonological dyslexics are able to read familiar but not unfamiliar words (although plausible), nor pronounceable non-words
impairment of the grapheme-phoneme conversion

## Reading impairments

### Acquired deep dislexia

semantic errors when reading words, e.g., CAT ---> dog
inability to read non-words
impairment of both grapheme-phoneme conversion, and lexical-semantical system 
typically accompanied by impairments to language abilities other than reading, as the damage in the brain seems to extend to a huge portion of the left hemisphere


# Language in the infant brain

## Research methods in infancy

* tasks that do not require verbal instructions or key-pressing responses
* short attention span
* get tired quickly
* experiments have to be fast (~5 minutes max)

Research with infants is challenging!

## Research methods in infancy

* Behavioral (based on infants' natural tendency to look at conspicuous/novel visual stimuli)
* Physiological (cardiac rhythm)
* Bain imaging (EEG, fMRI, MEG, fNIRS)

## Research methods in infancy

### Behavioural methods

change in behavioral response = ability to discriminate 2
events

## Research methods in infancy

### Behavioural methods

Headturn Preference Procedure (HPP) [Kemler-Nelson, 1995]

* familiarization with acoustic stimuli (e.g., sequence of sounds)
* then, 2 types of audio stimuli
* presented while a flashing light alternates on the lateral
screens
* infant would make head turns towards the light, and listen to
the sounds as long as she wants
* sound stops when baby stops looking


## Research methods in infancy

### Behavioural methods

Preferential looking

* Two images on a screen
* recording looking time at each image
* determines if infants can discriminate one stimulus from another by measuring how much time they look at them
* Images can be paired with sounds to measure acoustic preferences through visual preferences


## Research methods in infancy

### Behavioural methods

Preferential looking (eye-tracking)

* automatized recording of infant's eye-movements (eye-position, fixations, saccades..)
* based on infrared light (non-invasive) that create aa corneal reflection to locate eye position
* pupillometry

## Research methods in infancy

### Behavioural methods

Habituation / Dishabituation

* showing the same stimulus repeatedly until infant shows a clear decrease in looking time
* when a novel stimulus is presented, an increase in looking time should occur


## Research methods in infancy

### Behavioural methods

High-Amplitude Sucking Procedure

newborns is given a special pacifier that measures sucking rate

* newborn's sucking frequency controls the presentation of
sounds until bored (habituation)
* presentation of new sound: if newborn recognizes the change, she will increases the sucking rate

## Research methods in infancy

### Neuroimaging methods

A change in neurophisiological response contingent to different types of stimulation may reveal differences in underlying procecesing between stimulus types.

## Research methods in infancy

### Neuroimaging methods

Magnetoencephalography (MEG)

maps brain activity

* records magnetic fields caused by electrical
activity naturally produced in the brain
*  good at spatially localize brain activation
* pros: baby is free to move; good spatial resolution
* cons: huge, very expensive

## Research methods in infancy

### Neuroimaging methods

Functional Magnetic Resonance (fMRI)

* measures brain activity by detecting hemodynamic response in the brain
(changes in blood flow)
* cons: lot of noise, babies should move as less as possible as movements can cause artifacts (distortions of images)

## Research methods in infancy

### Neuroimaging methods

Electroencephalography (EEG)

records electrical activity naturally produced by the brain

* measures voltage fluctuations resulting from ionic current within neurons (ERPs) in response to stimuli (images, sounds etc)
* pros: cheaper; more baby-friendly than other techniques; good to measure timecourse of activation
* cons: also sensitive to motion

## Research methods in infancy

### Neuroimaging methods

Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS)

measures hemodynamic responses in the brain during stimuli presentation (images, sounds, etc)

* infrared light goes into the scalp and
comes back
* provides info about brain activation as amount of oxygen delivered by cerebral blood flow in a brain area
* pros: less invasive, less sensors


## Language acquisition

### At birth

At 2-3 days of life, neonate brain is already processing language, showing activation of main language areas.

## Language acquisition

### At birth

2- to 5- day-old neonates [@gomez2014]

* blif vs. lbif = possible vs. impossible syllables in all languages
* left temporal and right fronto-parietal areas activate when syllables are presented
* fNIRS measures differences in blood oxygen level in these areas in response to well-formed (possible) syllables vs. ill-formed (impossible) syllables

## Language acquisition

### Preference for speech 

at birth

* humans show a preference for native spoken language vs. acoustically similar, non-language stimuli (e.g., complex sequence of non-linguistic sounds) since birth
* preference for the vocalizations emitted by conspecifics is a common phenomenon in the animal kingdom
* for the young of different species, including infants, their own- species sounds (e.g., speech) have a “survival" importance

## Language acquisition

### Preference for speech 

at birth

DeCasper & Fifer, 1980; DeCasper & Spence, 1986;
for a review: Saffran, Werker & Werner, 2006

newborns prefer their mother's voice to other
female voices
* distinguish stories heard prenatally from other
stories
* prefer songs sang by the mother to other songs
* speech vs. synthetic sounds and white noise
* native speech vs. non-native speech


## Language acquisition

### Preference for speech

3 months -old [Shultz & Vouloumanos, 2010]

prefer non-native speech (e.g., Russian and
Japanese presented to English-learning infants) vs.
natural sounds sharing properties with spoken
languages:

* monkey calls
* human non-communicative vocalizations (e.g., sneezes)
* human communicative vocalizations (e.g., agreement)
* environmental sounds (e.g., running water)

## Language acquisition

### Preference for speech

3 months -old [Shultz & Vouloumanos, 2010]

these comparisons allowed to isolate some properties of
speech to see if infants' preferences are driven by any of them

[table]

* if infants' preferences were general, they would have preferred all biological sounds
* if infants' preferences were specific, they would have preferred speech (not all the other sounds)

## Language acquisition

### Preference for speech

3 months -old [Shultz & Vouloumanos, 2010]

Familiarity with speech does not drive the preference,
speech is non-native (Japanese and Russian)

## Language acquisition

### Language hemispheric dominance in infants

Pena et al. (2003). PNAS
left temporal region responds differently to s peech vs. backward speech vs. silence; right temporal region does not

greater activation in channels
7-12 on left hemisphere


## Language acquisition

### Language hemispheric dominance in infants

Dehaene-Lambertz et al. (2002). Science

fMRI study with 2- to 3-month-old infants shows activation of left
(not right) temporal and parietal areas in response to speech

## Prenatal experience with speech

fetuses do not experience speech as we do: only low-frequency components
of speech can be heard (pitch, rhythm, some phonetic information)

Eisenberg (1976); Gerhardt et al. (1992); Querleu et al., 1988; Lecaneut & Granier-Deferre (1993); Lasky & Trickey (2005)

## Prenatal experience with speech

fetuses have access to the mother's voice through bone
conduction:
* mother's voice is carried along the vertebral column into her pelvis to the bones of fetus' head, then directly to fetus' inner ear
* at ~36th weeks of gestation, fetal heart rate (FHR) decelerates and motor activity decreases when hearing sound of mother's voice

## Prenatal experience with speech

fetal heart rate (FHR) is also used in prenatal research to
investigate discrimination of sounds

* placing a loudspeaker close to the mom's abdomen
* FHR is measured with actograph or ultrasound visualization
* sound discrimination occurs when FHR changes (acceleration/deceleration of heart beat) in response to sound changes)
* used a lot in clinical research

## Prenatal experience with speech

May, Byers-Heinlein, Gervain & Werker (2011)

* research on fetal sound discrimination confirms the ability of fetuses to detect and respond to maternal voice
• mother's voice seems to be a salient auditory stimulus even
before birth, and has calming effect in fetuses
• effects on post-natal auditory preferences and behavior
